_sources: SMU MGMT102 Strategy, T2 AY25/26, sessions 1 to 11 and the week 1 to 7 revision cards

notes.term: Sustained competitive advantage comes from {{c1::analysis}}, then {{c2::formulation}}, then {{c3::implementation}}.
notes.definition: The AFI framework: diagnose the competitive challenge, set a guiding policy, then take coherent action.

notes.term: What are the three elements of a good strategy?
notes.definition: Strategic positioning, economic value creation, and strategic fit.
notes.example: Southwest: a clear low-cost position, value created at a price customers will pay, and activities that reinforce each other.

notes.term: Why is "be number one globally" not a strategy?
notes.definition: It is a goal with no diagnosis and no guiding policy. A strategy says where and how to compete, not how big to be.

notes.term: How is economic value created?
notes.definition: Perceived value, what a customer is willing to pay, minus the cost of providing the product or service.

notes.term: PESTEL scans {{c1::political}}, {{c2::economic}}, {{c3::social}}, {{c4::technological}}, {{c5::ecological}} and {{c6::legal}} forces.
notes.definition: The general environment: macro forces the firm has little control over, which shape industry-level forces in turn.

notes.term: Name Porter's five forces.
notes.definition: Threat of new entrants, threat of substitutes, bargaining power of buyers, bargaining power of suppliers, and rivalry among existing competitors.

notes.term: Complementors
notes.definition: The sixth force: firms whose products raise the value of yours, which is why competition and cooperation can run together as co-opetition.

notes.term: Strategic group
notes.definition: A set of firms in one industry following similar strategies. Profitability differs between groups, and mobility barriers make crossing hard.
notes.example: Hermes and Longchamp sit in different strategic groups within leather goods.

notes.term: How does CSV differ from CSR?
notes.definition: CSR is reactive and peripheral, usually philanthropy on an external agenda. CSV is proactive and integral, meeting a societal need through the core business, so it can link to competitive advantage.

notes.term: VRIO asks whether a resource is {{c1::valuable}}, {{c2::rare}}, {{c3::costly to imitate}}, and whether the firm is {{c4::organised to capture the value}}.
notes.definition: All four yes gives sustained competitive advantage. Some yes gives only a temporary one.

notes.term: Resource-based view
notes.definition: Explains performance differences by resource heterogeneity and immobility: firms hold different resources, and those resources do not move freely between them.

notes.term: How do resources, capabilities and core competencies differ?
notes.definition: Resources are the assets a firm can draw on. Capabilities are how those resources are bundled and deployed. Core competencies are the unique strengths that competitors cannot match and that link to advantage.

notes.term: What is the difference between value chain analysis and a strategic activity system?
notes.definition: Value chain analysis asks where value is created or lost, and is linear and standardised. A strategic activity system asks how activities interlock, and is a network unique to the firm. Individual activities can be copied; the web is what resists imitation.

notes.term: Isolating mechanisms
notes.definition: What protects an advantage from imitation over time, such as path dependence, causal ambiguity, social complexity, and intellectual property.

notes.term: What does "stuck in the middle" mean?
notes.definition: Committing to neither differentiation nor cost leadership, and so holding no clear strategic position. The two positions need different resources, capabilities and activities, which is why the trade-off is real.
notes.example: Tata Nano and Yahoo are the usual examples.

notes.term: The ERRC grid asks what to {{c1::eliminate}}, {{c2::reduce}}, {{c3::raise}} and {{c4::create}}.
notes.definition: Blue ocean strategy: value innovation, where the moves that create differentiation also drive cost down.
notes.example: IKEA eliminated sales staff, reduced warranties, raised accessibility, and created a new shopping experience.

notes.term: Why is cost minimisation not cost leadership?
notes.definition: Cost minimisation lowers the cost of providing a good without giving up the value position. Cost leadership offers the lowest price at an acceptable quality, and is a strategic position in itself.

notes.term: What does transaction cost economics decide?
notes.definition: Whether to make in-house or buy on the market, by comparing the cost of organising an activity internally against the cost of transacting for it, including principal-agent problems.

notes.term: A strategic resource gap can be closed by {{c1::building}} internally, {{c2::borrowing}} through an alliance, or {{c3::buying}} through an acquisition.
notes.definition: Prefer the cheaper, lower-risk option first. A resource that can simply be bought is rarely a source of sustained advantage.

notes.term: How does related diversification differ from unrelated?
notes.definition: Related businesses share core competencies, so the corporate parent can add value across them. Unrelated businesses, as in a conglomerate, share none, and the sum of the parts has to beat the parts standing alone.
notes.example: Amazon into AWS is related: the technology and data capability carries over.

notes.term: Roughly how much of performance difference do firm effects explain, against industry effects?
notes.definition: Firm effects explain up to about 55 percent, industry effects about 20 percent. Which is why internal analysis cannot be skipped.

notes.term: The marketing mix is {{c1::product}}, {{c2::price}}, {{c3::place}} and {{c4::promotion}}.
notes.definition: The set of tactical tools a firm blends to produce the response it wants from its target market.

notes.term: Market strategy runs {{c1::segmentation}}, then {{c2::targeting}}, then {{c3::positioning}}.
notes.definition: Split the market into groups, choose which to serve, then decide what to stand for in their minds.

notes.term: What are the three stages of the strategic marketing process?
notes.definition: Plan, implement, evaluate. Evaluation only matters if deviations are acted on.

notes.term: Product line
notes.definition: A group of related products that function in a similar way, are sold to the same customers, or fall in the same price range.

notes.term: How do product mix width and length differ?
notes.definition: Width is the number of different product lines the company carries. Length is the total number of items across those lines.

notes.term: Adopters arrive as {{c1::innovators}}, {{c2::early adopters}}, the {{c3::early majority}}, the {{c4::late majority}}, and {{c5::laggards}}.
notes.definition: The diffusion curve. The early majority are pragmatists who wait; laggards stay loyal to the status quo.

notes.term: Post-decision dissonance
notes.definition: The discomfort felt after choosing between close alternatives, which marketers answer with reassurance after the sale rather than before it.

notes.term: How does positive reinforcement differ from negative reinforcement?
notes.definition: Positive reinforcement adds a pleasant consequence after a response. Negative reinforcement removes an unpleasant one. Both increase the behaviour, which is what separates negative reinforcement from punishment.

notes.term: Observational learning
notes.definition: Learning a behaviour by watching others and the consequences they receive, rather than through direct experience of your own.

notes.term: When would you choose skimming over penetration pricing?
notes.definition: Skimming sets a high launch price to harvest customers who value the product most, and suits a genuine innovation with weak substitutes. Penetration sets a low price to buy share quickly, and suits a market where scale or a network effect decides the winner.

notes.term: What four characteristics separate services from products?
notes.definition: Intangibility, heterogeneity, inseparability of production and consumption, and perishability.
notes.hint: Cannot touch it, cannot standardise it, cannot separate it, cannot store it

notes.term: Brand extension
notes.definition: Using an established brand name to launch a product in a new category. It borrows the parent's equity, and it can damage that equity when the fit is poor.

notes.term: What are the four bases of market segmentation?
notes.definition: Geographic, demographic, psychographic and behavioural. Demographic is the most used, which is not the same as the most useful.

notes.term: Who counts as a direct competitor?
notes.definition: The firms customers perceive as close substitutes, not the ones that merely sell the same category. Perception decides the competitive set.
